title: Biofeedback-Inspired Algorithm Optimization
abstract: This paper explores the application of biofeedback control principles to optimize traditional algorithms. The core idea is to mimic the feedback control mechanisms inherent in biological neural systems to enhance the training and performance of these algorithms. Specifically, the algorithm parameter update process is mapped onto feedback loops within a simulated biological neural system. This approach leverages the inherent adaptive and robust nature of biofeedback, aiming to accelerate convergence and improve robustness of the algorithms. The methodology presented offers a novel approach to algorithm optimization, potentially overcoming limitations encountered in conventional optimization techniques. The paper details the conceptual framework, mathematical formulation, and potential benefits of this biofeedback-inspired optimization strategy.

title: Quantum Error Correction Code-Based Communication Protocol Optimization
abstract: This paper investigates the optimization of communication protocols leveraging the principles of quantum error correction codes (QECCs). The core claim is that by strategically designing and implementing QECCs within communication protocols, it is possible to significantly enhance communication reliability and efficiency. Specifically, we explore novel QECC designs and their application to improve the fault tolerance and data transmission rates of quantum communication systems. The research focuses on the practical application of QECCs, addressing a critical area for advancing the overall performance of quantum communication networks. The proposed approach aims to mitigate the detrimental effects of noise and decoherence, which are inherent challenges in quantum communication, thereby paving the way for more robust and reliable quantum data transmission. The presented methodology offers a framework for tailoring QECCs to specific communication scenarios, optimizing for both error correction performance and communication overhead.

title: 基于动态的量子势的计算
abstract: This paper presents a novel computational framework for quantum systems, leveraging dynamic quantum potentials to automatically adjust system parameters and enhance computational efficiency. Traditional approaches often rely on static quantum potential calculations, which suffer from inherent errors due to this static nature. This work introduces a method that dynamically adjusts parameters based on the evolving quantum potential, mitigating these errors and offering a significant improvement in the performance of quantum computations. The framework's core mechanism involves a continuous optimization process applied to the quantum potential, leading to more accurate and efficient results. We detail the algorithm, its implementation, and preliminary results demonstrating its effectiveness in a specific quantum simulation scenario.

title: Intermediate Task Difficulty and mT5's Zero-Shot Cross-Lingual Transfer Performance
abstract: Intermediate-task training---fine-tuning a pretrained model on an intermediate task before fine-tuning again on the target task---often improves model performance substantially on language understanding tasks in monolingual English settings. We investigate whether English intermediate-task training is still helpful on non-English target tasks. Using nine intermediate language-understanding tasks, we evaluate intermediate-task transfer in a zero-shot cross-lingual setting on the XTREME benchmark. title: A Globally Convergent Algorithm for Total Scaled-Gradient Variation via Cone-Constrained Bilinear Decomposition
abstract: The total scaled-gradient variation (TSGV) regularizer, derived from sparse modeling of piecewise-linear structures, has been shown to preserve edges and corners in image restoration. However, its highly nonconvex and nonlinear nature poses severe computational challenges, as existing methods often suffer from parameter sensitivity or lack convergence guarantees. To overcome this, we propose a tailored bilinear decomposition that decouples the nonlinear weighted gradient in the TSGV regularizer. This approach yields an equivalent optimization problem governed by cone or sphere constraints, depending on the chosen scaling function. In particular, the cone constraint plays a central role in characterizing edge- and corner-preserving behavior. We solve this reformulation using the alternating minimization method (AMM) equipped with a majorization--minimization strategy, ensuring a monotonic decrease in energy without step-size tuning. Furthermore, we provide a geometric interpretation of the edge-preserving properties of these constraints by analyzing their asymptotic behavior near image singularities. We establish the global convergence of the proposed method to a critical point within the Kurdyka--Łojasiewicz framework. Extensive numerical experiments on Gaussian denoising and non-line-of-sight (NLOS) imaging show that the proposed method achieves PSNR and SSIM competitive with or superior to representative variational methods, especially at high noise levels, and improves the structural reconstruction under dense and sparse scanning.

title: Adaptive Topology Mapping
abstract: This paper presents a novel adaptive topology mapping algorithm designed to dynamically adjust the topology of a system based on its internal state. Traditional methods often rely on static mappings, limiting the algorithm's flexibility and potential for optimization. Our approach leverages a self-adaptive process, allowing the topology to evolve in real-time to achieve enhanced control and performance. The core mechanism involves a feedback loop that continuously evaluates the system's state and adjusts the topology to mitigate errors and improve efficiency. This results in a more robust and responsive system. This work demonstrates the practical benefits of this dynamic topology modification through simulations and analysis, highlighting a significant improvement over existing approaches.

title: 基于动态拓扑的量子自适应计算
abstract: This paper introduces a novel quantum self-adaptive computing framework based on dynamic topology. Traditional quantum computation relies on the efficiency of classical computation, but this framework leverages quantum mechanics' inherent adaptability to significantly enhance computational efficiency. The framework utilizes a dynamically evolving topological structure to simulate learning processes, effectively optimizing the quantum algorithm's performance. The core mechanism centers on the dynamic adjustment of topological parameters, mirroring the iterative refinement of a machine learning model. We demonstrate the framework's efficacy through a series of numerical experiments, showcasing improved performance compared to traditional quantum algorithms in specific scenarios. The work presents a fundamentally new approach to quantum self-adaptation, offering a promising pathway towards more efficient and versatile quantum computation.

title: Title: Self-Aware Quantum Neural Networks for Enhanced Learning
abstract: Quantum neural networks (QNNs) hold immense potential for accelerating machine learning and tackling complex problems. However, current QNN architectures often lack the ability to dynamically adapt their parameters and strategies, limiting their effectiveness. This research explores the concept of self-aware quantum neural networks, a novel approach designed to dynamically adjust network parameters and learning pathways during training, ultimately enhancing learning efficiency and performance. We propose a framework utilizing quantum annealing to guide the network's self-improvement process, creating a self-aware learning mechanism. This work presents a theoretical framework and initial simulation results demonstrating the potential of this approach. The core claim is that these QNNs can exhibit self-awareness, allowing for dynamic parameter adjustment and strategic learning. This paper explores the potential benefits of this self-aware learning paradigm.

title: Symbolic Regression with Evolutionary Algorithms for Discovering Hidden Mathematical Relationships
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to discovering hidden mathematical relationships within datasets using evolutionary algorithms and symbolic regression. The core idea is to leverage the power of automated search to generate mathematical expressions that accurately represent the underlying data patterns. The method employs a genetic algorithm to evolve a population of mathematical expressions, iteratively refining them to minimize the error between the expression and the original data. Crucially, constraints are incorporated to manage the complexity of the expressions and steer the evolutionary process towards more interpretable and potentially meaningful relationships. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through a series of examples, showcasing its ability to uncover complex mathematical models from diverse datasets. The results highlight the potential of this technique to automate scientific discovery and provide insights into systems where the governing relationships are not immediately apparent.

title: Synthetic Biology-Inspired Computational Circuit Design via Genetic Algorithms
abstract: This paper explores the application of genetic algorithms (GAs), drawing inspiration from synthetic biology's evolutionary principles, to the design of complex computational circuits. The core concept involves representing circuit designs as "genes" and utilizing a GA framework—employing selection, crossover, and mutation operators—to iteratively refine and optimize circuit performance. We posit that this approach, mirroring biological evolution, offers a novel pathway toward generating innovative circuit architectures and functionalities. The fitness function, central to the GA process, is explicitly defined to evaluate circuit performance based on relevant metrics. This work presents a theoretical framework and outlines the methodology for such an approach, demonstrating its potential for automated and highly effective circuit design. The algorithm's effectiveness is demonstrated through the design of a simulated circuit, showcasing the GA's ability to converge on solutions with optimized characteristics. Further research will focus on incorporating real-world constraints and exploring the scalability of this method for larger and more complex circuit designs.

title: Dynamic Programming with Probabilistic State Spaces for Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Traditional dynamic programming (DP) methods face significant challenges when applied to reinforcement learning (RL) problems characterized by continuous and stochastic state spaces. This paper proposes a novel dynamic programming algorithm designed to overcome these limitations. The core idea is to adaptively discretize the state space based on the underlying probability distributions. This approach enables efficient exploration and provides a means to approximate solutions within complex, high-dimensional RL environments. The algorithm introduces a probabilistic state representation, fundamentally changing how DP operates and broadening its applicability to a wider range of RL scenarios. We outline the key components of the algorithm and discuss its potential benefits and challenges.

title: Differential Privacy for Federated Learning with Personalized Noise
abstract: Federated learning (FL) offers a promising approach to training machine learning models on decentralized data, preserving data privacy. However, traditional differential privacy (DP) mechanisms often introduce significant noise into the global model updates, leading to substantial accuracy degradation. This paper presents a novel personalized differential privacy (P-DP) scheme for FL, where the noise level is dynamically adjusted based on the sensitivity of individual user data. We introduce a method for calculating per-user sensitivity values, considering local data distributions, and then employ adaptive noise scaling to minimize the privacy-utility trade-off. The proposed approach aims to achieve a better balance between privacy guarantees and model accuracy compared to standard DP methods in FL. The core contribution lies in the personalized allocation of the differential privacy budget, optimizing the system for a given application. Experimental results, although not presented here due to the focus on the method itself, would demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach.

title: Core Claim
abstract: Quantum entanglement presents a unique opportunity for secure communication due to its fundamental properties. This paper explores the potential of leveraging this entanglement for quantum key distribution (QKD) protocols. We propose a novel protocol that exploits the self-related properties of entangled particles to guarantee key security. This work details the design of a QKD protocol centered around this self-correlation, aiming to improve key distribution security and efficiency. The paper presents a comprehensive overview of the protocol's design, mathematical foundations, and potential benefits.

title: Quantum-Inspired Optimization for Large-Scale Combinatorial Problems
abstract: Large-scale combinatorial optimization problems, arising in diverse fields such as logistics, finance, and operations research, pose a significant challenge to classical optimization algorithms. These problems typically involve searching through an exponentially large solution space, making exhaustive search methods computationally intractable. This paper proposes a novel quantum-inspired optimization algorithm designed to address this challenge. The algorithm leverages techniques inspired by amplitude estimation, a core concept in quantum computing, to accelerate the search process. Specifically, we employ a Monte Carlo-based approach that utilizes amplitude estimation to efficiently sample from the probability distribution governing the solution space. The resulting algorithm demonstrates promising performance in tackling large-scale combinatorial problems, offering a computationally efficient alternative to traditional optimization methods. We demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness through theoretical analysis and provide insights into its advantages and limitations. The primary goal is to provide a viable method for tackling complex optimization tasks, drawing inspiration from quantum principles without the need for full quantum hardware.

title: 基于量子纠缠的分布式计算
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a bizarre phenomenon where two or more particles become linked in such a way that they share the same fate no matter how far apart they are, has captivated scientists and engineers for decades. Harnessing this quantum phenomenon offers the potential for revolutionary advancements in computation, particularly in the realm of distributed computing. This paper explores the development of a novel distributed computing framework based on quantum entanglement, aiming to significantly enhance computational efficiency through the exploitation of entanglement's unique properties. We detail the core mechanism, outlining the design and implementation of this framework, and highlight the key advantages it offers over existing approaches. This work contributes to the burgeoning field of quantum computing and distributed systems, pushing the boundaries of what's computationally feasible.

title: Source-Preserving Prompt Augmentation and Category-Adaptive Inference for Qwen3-1.7B: A Prospective Seed-Replication Study
abstract: This preprint investigates whether a fixed compound inference intervention can improve the performance of a small language model without updating its parameters. The experimental program compares structured prompt replacement, natural-language rewriting, source-preserving semantic augmentation, and a category-adaptive Qwen inference profile. Evaluation uses 48 IFBench and 48 LiveBench tasks with research-authored semantic-stress variants, programmatic scorers, pinned model and benchmark revisions, and matched stochastic seeds.In the prospectively specified P1.3 seed replication, Qwen3-1.7B improved from a mean objective score of 0.272 under raw non-thinking inference to 0.360 under source-preserving augmentation combined with category-adaptive inference. The paired effect was +0.088 (95% percentile-bootstrap CI: 0.018 to 0.160). Component analysis found a positive adaptive-inference-profile effect of +0.061, while the incremental contribution of semantic augmentation under matched adaptive inference remained uncertain at +0.027 (95% CI: −0.046 to 0.099).The study confirms the complete intervention on the fixed 96-task set under new stochastic draws; it does not establish independent task-level replication, cross-model generalization, or semantic augmentation as the active causal component. The package also increased prompt length, latency, and test-time computation. Version 1.1 provides detailed inference settings, benchmark identifiers, systems-cost accounting, causal boundaries, representative interventions, and reproducibility information.

Evaluation uses 48 IFBench and 48 LiveBench tasks with research-authored semantic-stress variants, programmatic scorers, pinned model and benchmark revisions, and matched stochastic seeds.In the prospectively specified P1.3 seed replication, Qwen3-1.7B improved from a mean objective score of 0.272 under raw non-thinking inference to 0.360 under source-preserving augmentation combined with category-adaptive inference. The paired effect was +0.088 (95% percentile-bootstrap CI: 0.018 to 0.160). Component analysis found a positive adaptive-inference-profile effect of +0.061, while the incremental contribution of semantic augmentation under matched adaptive inference remained uncertain at +0.027 (95% CI: −0.046 to 0.099).The study confirms the complete intervention on the fixed 96-task set under new stochastic draws; it does not establish independent task-level replication, cross-model generalization, or semantic augmentation as the active causal component. The package also increased prompt length, latency, and test-time computation. Version 1.1 provides detailed inference settings, benchmark identifiers, systems-cost accounting, causal boundaries, representative interventions, and reproducibility information.

title: FIREQ: FPGA Instrumentation for Readout and Qubit control
abstract: We present FIREQ (FPGA Instrumentation for Readout and Qubit control), an open-source RFSoC-based framework for the control and readout of superconducting qubits. FIREQ combines a modular AXI-compliant firmware architecture with a PYNQ-based software stack designed to support extensible hardware integration, deterministic experiment timing, and low-overhead execution of repeated calibration and characterization workflows. The firmware implements direct RF synthesis and acquisition, trigger-based sequencing, programmable pulse generation, frequency-multiplexed readout, and memory-efficient acquisition and waveform buffering. The software adopts a client-server architecture with streamed data transfer and dependency-aware configuration updates to reduce host-device and reconfiguration overhead during parameter sweeps. On an AMD Zynq UltraScale+ RFSoC ZCU216, FIREQ generates RF pulses up to 9.3 GHz with a pulse-duration resolution of 107 ps and an event-timing resolution of 1.7 ns. FPGA resource utilization is compared with representative open-source RFSoC control frameworks, showing a low BRAM footprint while retaining full-rate I/Q generation and acquisition. The RF output is characterized in terms of phase noise, noise spectral density, and inter-channel timing skew. End-to-end operation is validated on a superconducting qubit through resonator spectroscopy, Rabi, Ramsey, and relaxation measurements, yielding T1 = 6.94 us and T2* = 13.50 us. FIREQ can therefore be used both as a qubit-control platform and as an experimental environment for evaluating alternative control and readout IP architectures.

title: Neural video codecs quality assessment dataset and benchmark
abstract: Video traffic constitutes a significant share of global web traffic. To reduce its volume, video codecs have been developed and continuously improved. While the industry has achieved substantial progress in traditional video coding, neural video codecs (NVCs) have recently emerged as a new approach that applies deep learning to video compression. This creates new challenges for compression quality assessment, which is essential for the further development and improvement of such codecs. In particular, it is important to evaluate the novel temporal compression paradigms introduced by NVCs. In this work, we present a large-scale subjective dataset of videos compressed with both neural and traditional video codecs. The subjective scores were collected through crowd-sourced pairwise comparisons. The proposed dataset provides a valuable resource for the development and benchmarking of video quality metrics tailored to neural video codecs. The dataset is available at the following link: https://videoprocessing.github.io/nvc-dataset-benchmark

title: APIFlow-Bench: Measuring Whether Agents Survive Long, Dependent API Workflows
abstract: Tool-using agents are commonly evaluated by a single bit: whether an end-to-end workflow completed. This metric fails to distinguish failures that matter in production, such as expired credentials, malformed payloads, or correct execution followed by incorrect final delivery. We introduce APIFlow-Bench, a fully auditable benchmark for long-horizon, dependent REST-API workflows that decomposes performance into seven engineering capabilities and requires agents to produce answers supported by the actual call path. We generate synthetic API worlds forward, subtask by subtask; each subtask is admitted only after a zero-LLM self-test triad verifies its grader and an oracle establishes solvability, and an adversarial audit identified and fixed six grader exploits. Grading is deterministic and provenance-sensitive: a state check traces a mock-minted canary through the API data flow to the response the answer must originate from, and a typed answer card is verified field by field. We release all answer keys and 44,362 unredacted execution transcripts. Across 19 frontier and open-weight models under one neutral scaffold, we find: (1) longer dependency chains degrade success, from 93% on individual subtasks to 74% on clean 20-subtask chains and 61% when including the 8% of chain trials that a model-consensus screen flags as passed by no model; (2) reliability separates models more than best-case capability, with best-of-five spanning seven points but all-five-of-five reliability spanning 44 points; (3) the independent-error account of compounding failure does not fit the data: pass rates on 20-subtask chains are 33 percentage points above the product of subtask-level rates, and on the clean slice 77% of failing runs reached the correct final state and failed only at delivery.

title: Self-Organizing Graph Neural Networks via Competitive Learning
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to graph clustering utilizing self-organizing Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) based on competitive learning. Traditional graph clustering methods often necessitate labeled data, introducing bias and limiting applicability in scenarios with unlabeled graphs. Our method circumvents this limitation by employing a competitive learning dynamic within the GNN architecture. Each node in the graph simultaneously attempts to represent its local neighborhood, with the winning representation propagating forward. This competitive process fosters an emergent discovery of graph structure and facilitates effective node clustering. We demonstrate that this approach can achieve significant clustering performance without explicit labels, offering a potentially more robust and adaptable solution for graph analysis. The core mechanism is described in detail, highlighting the mathematical formulation of the competitive learning process and its impact on representation learning. The key innovation lies in the dynamic adaptation of node representations through competition, leading to a self-organized graph structure.

title: Latent Space Modeling for Symbolic Representation Learning
abstract: This paper explores the application of latent space modeling for symbolic representation learning. We propose a framework that leverages the power of latent space models, specifically variational autoencoders (VAEs), to map data into a lower-dimensional latent space. Subsequently, we employ symbolic representation techniques to transform the information within this latent space into discrete, symbolic representations. The core claim is that this approach enables efficient learning of high-level features within the data, facilitating symbolic reasoning. The novelty lies in the synergistic combination of latent space learning and symbolic representation, offering a pathway to effectively represent complex data in a manner conducive to symbolic manipulation and inference. We demonstrate the potential of this method through theoretical analysis and conceptual framework, outlining a future direction for research in this area.

title: Knowledge Graph Construction Based on Semantic Network Reasoning
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to knowledge graph construction leveraging semantic network reasoning. Traditional knowledge graph construction methods often rely heavily on manual annotation or rule-based systems, which are both labor-intensive and prone to inaccuracies. Our approach utilizes semantic network reasoning algorithms to automatically extract knowledge from unstructured data. Specifically, we perform semantic analysis and relation extraction on unstructured text, constructing a semantic network to represent the extracted knowledge. This network is then transformed into a knowledge graph. The core of our method lies in the automated discovery of implicit relationships within the data, leading to a more complete and accurate knowledge graph compared to methods relying solely on explicit information. We present a framework for this process, detailing the key steps and algorithms involved. The resulting knowledge graph offers a robust and scalable solution for knowledge representation and reasoning.

title: Quantum Entanglement-Based Information Encoding and Decoding via Bio-Inspired Algorithms
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to quantum entanglement-based information encoding and decoding, drawing inspiration from biological neural networks. The core concept leverages the plasticity of synapses and the quantum entanglement properties between neurons to enhance the reliability of information transmission. Specifically, we simulate synaptic plasticity to dynamically modulate entanglement states, employing a biologically-inspired search algorithm to optimize these states for robust encoding and decoding. The algorithm's key innovation lies in the synergistic combination of biological mechanisms with quantum phenomena, offering a potentially more efficient and resilient framework for quantum information processing compared to traditional approaches. We present a theoretical framework outlining the algorithm's operation, detailing the mathematical formulation of the entanglement manipulation process and the optimization strategy. The proposed method holds promise for applications in secure communication, quantum sensing, and potentially, a deeper understanding of the interplay between quantum mechanics and biological systems.

title: Dynamic Quantum Entanglement: Adaptive Computation
abstract: Quantum entanglement is a fundamental phenomenon in quantum mechanics, exhibiting correlations between distant particles that defy classical intuition. Its inherent fragility makes it challenging to utilize for complex computations. This paper explores the application of dynamic quantum entanglement to adaptive computation, offering a novel approach to tackling problems requiring intricate and evolving quantum states. We propose a method that leverages the self-correlation of entangled states to dynamically adjust the state of the entanglement, enabling computations that respond to changes in the system's environment. The core claim is that a dynamically adjusted entanglement can facilitate more efficient and robust solutions for specific computational tasks. The investigation incorporates a conceptual framework, detailed mathematical models, and preliminary experimental results demonstrating the potential of this approach. This research addresses a significant challenge in quantum computing – the need for computational flexibility – by introducing a new mechanism for manipulating entanglement.

title: Quantum Networks Based Multi-Party Secure Computation Protocol
abstract: This paper presents a novel protocol for secure multi-party computation (SMC) leveraging quantum networks and quantum key distribution (QKD). The core idea is to utilize the inherent security properties of QKD and quantum states to construct a secure computational environment, safeguarding the privacy of participants during distributed calculations. The protocol, termed Quantum Network-Based SMC (QN-SMC), employs a layered approach combining a classical pre-processing phase with a quantum computation phase secured by QKD. We detail the protocol's architecture, mathematical formulations, and security guarantees. The key contributions of this work lie in the integration of QKD into the SMC framework, enabling computation on distributed quantum states while maintaining confidentiality and integrity. We explore the feasibility and potential impact of this approach for applications requiring secure distributed processing within a quantum network. The protocol's performance is analyzed in terms of key distribution rates, computational overhead, and security levels.

title: Adaptive Quantum Algorithms for Optimization
abstract: This paper explores the development of adaptive quantum algorithms designed to optimize the performance of quantum algorithms. The core concept involves dynamically adjusting parameters such as qubit coupling strength and measurement time, based on the algorithm's runtime behavior. This is achieved through the application of reinforcement learning, where an agent learns to optimize these parameters in response to metrics like decoherence and measurement error. The research addresses a significant challenge in quantum algorithm design – the difficulty in determining optimal parameter values – and presents a novel approach for achieving superior performance. The framework outlined herein provides a pathway for creating more robust and efficient quantum algorithms across a range of applications.

title: Adaptive Incremental Learning for Robot Motion Planning
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to robot motion planning based on adaptive incremental learning. The core idea is to leverage the strengths of both reinforcement learning and incremental learning to achieve efficient and accurate motion planning. Traditional motion planning methods often suffer from computational complexity and difficulty in adapting to dynamic environments. This work proposes a motion planning controller built upon reinforcement learning, which learns optimal trajectories through interaction with the environment. Crucially, an adaptive incremental learning mechanism is integrated to allow the controller to quickly adapt to changes in the environment or task constraints without requiring retraining from scratch. The proposed method significantly improves the efficiency and precision of motion planning, particularly in scenarios with evolving dynamics. The paper outlines the theoretical framework, the design of the controller, and the implementation details, demonstrating its effectiveness through a conceptual analysis and outlining potential future research directions.

title: How Do We Know They Work? A Systematic Review of Evaluation Practices and Methodological Rigor in LLM-Based Agentic Educational Systems
abstract: Background. Large language model (LLM) based agentic educational systems, which plan, use tools, reflect, or coordinate as multiple agents, are proliferating, but whether they are evaluated rigorously enough to support claims about learning is unclear.Objective. To systematically characterize the evaluation practices and methodological rigor of LLM-based agentic educational systems, and to derive a reporting standard for the field.Methods. Following PRISMA 2020, I searched eight sources (Scopus, Web of Science, ACM, IEEE, ERIC, ACL Anthology, arXiv, EdArXiv) for empirical studies of agentic educational systems published from January 2023 to June 2026. A single reviewer screened 3,710 deduplicated records, assisted by a validated advisory LLM triage (blind human-AI agreement Cohen’s κ = 0.65–0.74) that recommended but never determined decisions. Of 477 included studies, the 132 with openly retrievable full text were coded against a 41-field rigor-and-reporting codebook; 129 agentic studies formed the analytic set.Results. Evaluation was predominantly output-oriented: 56.6% used no human learners and only 23.3% measured an actual learning outcome. Rigor and reproducibility were limited: 1.6% used fully validated instruments, 2.3% controlled for novelty effects, 17.8% were fully reproducible, and 50.4% released prompts. Appraisal-critical reporting was sparse (ethics/IRB unreported in 68.2%). Studies disclosed most items (mean 16.2/18) but met far fewer in practice.Conclusions. The field is closer to a transparency norm than a rigor norm. I propose the Agentic Educational AI Evaluation and Reporting (AEER) checklist, a disclosure-focused reporting standard targeting these gaps at low cost. Findings pertain to the open-access subset and are preliminary.

title: Scaffold-Conditioned Evidence Weighting for Misconception Tracking: A Sealed-Truth Synthetic Validation
abstract: Adaptive learning systems that track misconception mastery face a fundamental identification challenge: scaffolded responses carry less diagnostic information than unscaffolded ones, yet most Bayesian knowledge tracing (BKT) implementations weight all evidence equally. We introduce a tempered evidence update that conditions BKT transition weights on scaffold type, and validate it in a 36-cell full-factorial synthetic experiment (n=500 learners per cell — 18,000 total — 30 constructs, 12 sessions). The design crosses four factors, response richness (sparse/medium/rich), avoidance propensity (low/medium/high), noise level (low/high), and session-effect correlation (low/high), using common random numbers for cross-cell comparability. Across all 36 cells, the Depth Engine achieves AUC 0.898–0.953 at the final checkpoint, with fact-validity ratios (FVR) of 1.0%–2.0% and median closure at session 5.0 (target: 5–7). The engine's tempered update outperforms its untempered ablation in all 36 cells (Wilcoxon W = 666, p < 1.5 x 10^-11; mean ΔAUC = +0.005, range +0.002 to +0.008) and terminal-score baselines by 6.4 percentage points, while BKT with EM-fitted parameters provides a strong oracle-assisted reference (AUC 0.937–0.969). One cell (sparse evidence, high noise, low avoidance) falls below AUC 0.90, reaching 0.898; the remaining 35 cells exceed 0.90. These results establish that scaffold-conditioned evidence weighting is a viable approach to misconception tracking in the presence of avoidance, noisy responses, and reopening dynamics.

title: Diagnosis of Oral Cancer from Histopathological Images Using Fusion of Dual Head Attention Mechanism with Gated Hybrid Second Order Residual Descriptor
abstract: Histopathology can help doctors find oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) early and accurately, which can help them avoid overtreatment and missed diagnoses.To provide an attention-enhanced, stain-aware framework that integrates robust pre-processing with.dual-order feature mapping and large-margin classification to provide dependable, calibrated predictions from 100× fields of vision.A dual-head mapping combines attention-weighted Generalized Mean pooling with a gated Hybrid Second-Order-Residual Descriptor (HSORD).The HSORD combines matrix-square-root covariance with NetVLAD residuals.A multi-prototype ArcFace head enforces angular margins makes the classes more compact and stable for aggregation by a nuclei-guided attention MIL.The proposed system achieves Receiver Operating Characteristic Area Under Curve (ROC-AUC) 0.973 and PR-AUC 0.969 with low Expected Calibration Error (0.018) on a public dataset (5,192 images; two institutions; 100×).The findings suggest that stain awareness, nuclei-guided attention, and dual-order statistics provide a synergistic trifecta for functional OSCC histopathology AI, providing interpretable focus maps and ready-to-use calibration.

title: Lightweight Quantum Convolutional Neural Networks via U (1)‐Equivariant Kernels and Information‐Guided Pooling
abstract: ABSTRACT While Quantum Convolutional Neural Networks (QCNNs) offer a structured framework for data processing in the noisy intermediate‐scale quantum (NISQ) regime, conventional architectures often rely on over‐parameterized ansätze that hinder trainability and increase sensitivity to hardware noise. Furthermore, standard quantum pooling strategies frequently discard useful coherent correlations. To address these limitations, we propose a parameter‐efficient QCNN architecture integrating a ‐equivariant convolutional ( Eq‐Conv ) kernel with a guided variational pooling ( Guided Var‐Pool ) scheme. By enforcing continuous symmetry via Schur's Lemma, the Eq‐Conv kernel requires only five trainable parameters, significantly reducing circuit complexity compared to full‐rank operations while maintaining competitive expressivity. For dimensionality reduction, the Guided Var‐Pool introduces an Information‐Bottleneck‐inspired penalty that actively drives discarded qubits toward the ground state, ensuring task‐relevant features are concentrated within the retained subsystem prior to truncation. To maintain NISQ compatibility, the architecture strictly adheres to the Principle of Deferred Measurement, eliminating the need for mid‐circuit measurements. Numerical experiments on MNIST and Fashion‐MNIST datasets demonstrate that our approach achieves competitive classification accuracy while exhibiting superior robustness against depolarizing noise. Compared to over‐parameterized baselines, the proposed model establishes a favorable depth‐for‐robustness trade‐off, providing a resource‐efficient pathway for scalable quantum machine learning.

title: Artificial Intelligence in a Photonic Temporal Processor
abstract: Optical neural networks (ONNs) promise high-throughput and energy-efficient artificial intelligence, yet essentially all implementations so far encode information across space either in free-space arrays or in integrated waveguide meshes, tying the number of neurons to the number of physical components and fixes the routing topology at fabrication. Here we show that moving the computation into time decouples computational dimension from hardware dimension. Exploiting space-time duality, we implement optical diffraction and interference entirely in time domain, using thin-film lithium niobate modulators as time lenses and temporal masks, with chromatic dispersion providing the coupling between successive temporal neurons. We experimentally verify high-order, complex-valued matrix-matrix multiplications using just a single optical input/output port, scaling the computational dimensions far beyond the channel count. By incorporating optical feedback, we extend this platform into versatile neural networks, where the network layers, neuron numbers, and synaptic connections are fully programmable and in-situ trainable. Our temporal diffractive neural networks are successfully validated on various classification benchmarks, alongside image and video generation tasks. Notably, using this platform we demonstrate an all-analogue generative pipeline in which the latent variable is drawn directly from amplified spontaneous emission, so that no digital sampling or electronic modulation appears anywhere in the generative path. Furthermore, high-resolution images and videos are generated at high frame rates, outperforming state-of-the-art modulator-refresh-limited optical generative systems. These results establish a unified photonic temporal computing framework, providing a scalable and deployable pathway toward next-generation machine intelligence.

title: Beyond Correctness: Validity-Oriented Evaluation of Biomedical LLM Judges
abstract: We propose a scalable, validity-oriented pipeline for evaluating biomedical LLM judges when high-quality human judgments are scarce. First, we augment existing human-labelled biomedical benchmarks with deterministic, metric-grounded mutations that produce auditable preference pairs. Second, we evaluate judges beyond aggregate correctness using three deployment-relevant dimensions: correctness against metric-derived gold labels, robustness under repeated stochastic sampling, and compliance with the requested output format. We use this pipeline to assess Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct under four regimes: (1) base, using the instruct model as is; (2) SFT, distillation-based supervised fine-tuning only; (3) RL, GRPO-based reinforcement learning only; and (4) SFT$\rightarrow$RL, SFT followed by RL. The base and single-stage regimes struggle on structured medical discrimination such as PICO extraction and clinical calculations, whereas SFT$\rightarrow$RL performs best across correctness, compliance, and robustness; gains concentrate on decomposable tasks (PICO, MedCalc), at times matching or outperforming frontier models.

title: Topological-Quantum Entanglement Probability Model
abstract: This paper introduces a novel probabilistic model predicated on topological-quantum entanglement, aiming to simulate the evolution of entangled states and automatically adjust entanglement parameters. The model leverages the inherent complexity of topological entanglement to provide a framework for quantifying and manipulating the dynamics of these states. We present a methodology for constructing this model and demonstrate its potential for generating and analyzing complex entangled configurations. This research addresses a key challenge in quantum information theory: the difficulty in accurately modeling and controlling entanglement. The proposed model offers a fundamentally different approach to entanglement analysis, potentially unlocking new avenues in quantum algorithms and quantum data processing.

title: Generalized Probability Model Integration
abstract: This paper introduces a novel Generalized Probability Model (GPM) framework, termed "Generalized Probability Model Integration" (GPMI), designed to enhance the generalization capabilities of probabilistic models. The core of this approach lies in the integration of knowledge graphs, specifically probability trees, to represent and fuse diverse probability distributions. A dynamic probability update mechanism is employed to continuously refine the model's parameters, leading to improved performance in complex scenarios. This work addresses a critical limitation of existing GPMs – their reliance on static probability distributions – by providing a mechanism for knowledge transfer and adaptive learning. We detail the architecture of the GPMI, the algorithm for knowledge graph construction and fusion, and the iterative update process, demonstrating its potential for robust and scalable probabilistic modeling. The focus is on achieving a deeper understanding of the relationships between different probability distributions through a structured knowledge representation.

title: Adaptive Learning Rate Scheduling based on Gradient Magnitude and Variance
abstract: This paper presents a novel adaptive learning rate scheduling method designed to address the limitations of conventional learning rate schedules in modern deep learning. The core issue addressed is the failure of existing schedules to effectively respond to the diverse nature of gradients encountered during training, leading to suboptimal convergence and potentially unstable training dynamics. Our approach introduces a dynamic adjustment of the learning rate predicated on both the magnitude and variance of the gradients. By explicitly considering both these factors, the method aims to simultaneously accelerate convergence and maintain stability. We demonstrate that this combined approach results in more robust and efficient training compared to traditional methods, particularly in scenarios with high variance or rapidly changing gradients. The method is described in detail, including the mathematical formulation and the key parameters involved, and its potential benefits are highlighted through theoretical analysis and a clear explanation of the underlying principles.

title: Based on Quantum Entanglement: A Distributed Computing Architecture
abstract: This paper proposes a novel distributed computing architecture leveraging the principles of quantum entanglement for enhanced parallel computation. Traditional distributed computing relies heavily on classical communication, which introduces latency and bandwidth limitations. This architecture aims to overcome these challenges by exploiting the inherent correlations within entangled quantum states. We introduce a framework where multiple computational nodes are interconnected via entangled qubits, forming a quantum entanglement network. This network facilitates direct, correlated computation between nodes, theoretically enabling a significant speedup compared to conventional parallel processing. The core claim of this work is the realization of ultra-efficient parallel computation through entanglement-based distributed computing. The presented model details the architecture, the entanglement management strategy, and the theoretical computational advantages. We focus on the conceptual design and the underlying mathematical framework, providing a foundation for future research and development in this area. The key mathematical concept driving this architecture is the manipulation of entangled states to perform computations without the need for direct data transfer between nodes. This approach presents a fundamentally different paradigm for distributed computing, with the potential to revolutionize fields reliant on computationally intensive tasks.

title: Quantum Entanglement-Based Physical Simulation Algorithm
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a bizarre phenomenon where two or more particles become linked in such a way that they share the same fate no matter how far apart they are, has captivated physicists and philosophers alike. Harnessing this quantum connection offers a potentially revolutionary approach to physical simulation, surpassing the limitations of classical computational methods. This paper proposes a novel physical simulation algorithm predicated on the principles of quantum entanglement, aiming to achieve unprecedented accuracy in simulating complex quantum systems. We outline the core mechanism, detail the theoretical foundations, and explore the potential implications of this approach. The core claim centers around the design of a quantum entanglement-based algorithm capable of revealing subtle physical laws and offering a fundamentally deeper understanding of quantum phenomena.

title: Dynamic Topology Field Analysis: Adaptive Quantum Algorithm Optimization
abstract: Abstract: This paper introduces a novel dynamic topology field analysis algorithm designed to optimize quantum algorithms through adaptive parameter adjustment based on input data. Traditional quantum algorithm analysis often relies on static approaches, struggling with complex problems. We propose a method that leverages the inherent dynamic nature of topology to dynamically adjust quantum algorithm parameters, offering precise control and optimization. This paper details the core mechanism and its potential impact on quantum algorithm performance.

title: Topological Quantum States-Based Entanglement Preservation for Quantum Error Correction
abstract: This paper proposes a novel quantum error correction code leveraging the inherent entanglement preservation properties of topological quantum states. Traditional quantum error correction schemes rely on creating and maintaining fragile quantum entanglement, which is highly susceptible to environmental noise. Our approach utilizes the topologically protected nature of certain quantum states to provide a robust mechanism for error detection and correction. We formulate a code based on the controlled-Z operation within a topological qubit architecture, demonstrating a significant improvement in error correction capabilities compared to conventional approaches. Specifically, we define the code parameters, including the code rate, minimum distance, and the required number of physical qubits. We analyze the code's performance under various noise models, highlighting the enhanced resilience due to topological protection. The key innovation lies in harnessing the natural, robust entanglement provided by topological states, offering a pathway to more practical and reliable quantum computation. The theoretical framework presented here provides a foundation for future research and development in topological quantum error correction.

title: Adaptive Topological Self-Association Models
abstract: This paper presents a novel model, the Adaptive Topological Self-Association Models (ATSAM), designed to enhance the efficiency of data modeling and simulation. Traditional parameter adjustment methods often require manual intervention, limiting the model's adaptability. The ATSAM employs a dynamic mechanism that leverages the inherent topology of input data and its associated features to automatically adjust model parameters, resulting in more effective modeling and simulation capabilities. The core claim highlights the model's ability to dynamically adjust parameters based on data structure, improving efficiency compared to static parameter adjustment techniques. This research focuses on the concept of "Self-Association," where the model learns and adapts to the underlying topology of the input data.

title: Explainable AI for Graph Neural Networks via Symbolic Representation Learning
abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have demonstrated remarkable success in various domains, including social network analysis, drug discovery, and recommendation systems. However, their inherent complexity often leads to a "black box" problem, where it is difficult to understand the reasoning behind their predictions. This paper introduces a novel approach to explain GNN predictions by learning symbolic representations of the graph structure. We propose a model that maps the GNN's activations to a symbolic representation, enabling the generation of human-readable explanations. This method addresses the interpretability challenge in GNNs, offering a pathway to trust and confidence in their predictions. The core claim is that by leveraging symbolic representation learning, we can transform opaque GNN behavior into understandable insights. The proposed mechanism provides a foundation for building more transparent and reliable GNN-based systems.

title: Quantum-Enhanced Wave Function Collapse for Simulation
abstract: Quantum-enhanced wave function collapse provides a novel approach to simulation, leveraging quantum mechanics to expedite the process of determining the most probable state of a wave function. title: Adversarial Robustness in Zero-Shot Cross-Lingual Transfer Models Post-English QA Training
abstract: Intermediate-task training---fine-tuning a pretrained model on an intermediate task before fine-tuning again on the target task---often improves model performance substantially on language understanding tasks in monolingual English settings. We investigate whether English intermediate-task training is still helpful on non-English target tasks. Using nine intermediate language-understanding tasks, we evaluate intermediate-task transfer in a zero-shot cross-lingual setting on the XTREME benchmark. title: Universal Reconfigurable Diffractive Photonic Chip for Multi‐Modal Optical Computing
abstract: ABSTRACT Optical computing represents a transformative hardware paradigm for the post‐Moore era, exploiting its inherent advantages of high speed, low power consumption, and intrinsic parallelism. Nonetheless, state‐of‐the‐art integrated optical computing systems suffer from critical limitations, including fixed functionality, single input modality, and restricted input scalability, which severely constrain their adaptability in dynamic application scenarios and their capability for high‐dimensional data loading. In this work, we present a universal reconfigurable diffractive photonic chip (URDPC) that enables adaptive processing of on‐chip transverse electric modes, free‐space structured light fields, electrical logic signals, and high‐dimensional task reasoning. Our architecture supports dynamic optical mode routing and sorting, as well as both homogeneous and heterogeneous parallel logic operations. By implementing an on‐chip data loading scheme that directly encodes high‐dimensional data into the reconfigurable modulation units of the chip, we demonstrate 84% classification accuracy on a four‐class MNIST task, effectively alleviating the inherent trade‐off between input dimensionality and data volume. Our results establish a promising technical route toward building high‐performance, highly flexible integrated intelligent photonic computing systems for multi‐modal information processing.

title: Efficient Language-to-Vision Feature Injection for Referring Single-Object Tracking
abstract: Referring single-object tracking enables language-grounded target initialization and subsequent tracking by jointly leveraging semantic cues and visual templates. The core difficulty is to use language differently across stages: it is indispensable for grounding but can induce semantic drift during tracking when overemphasized. Meanwhile, current methods often require costly vision-language alignment training. We present LVTrack, a pure transformer framework that introduces a mode-conditioned Gated Feature Injector to adaptively regulate textual guidance and alleviate semantic drift. Together with targeted adaptations, it directly harnesses a frozen vision-language pretrained model, greatly reducing training cost and preserving strong language understanding. To further improve temporal localization, LVTrack integrates hybrid relative-absolute positional encodings with a lightweight memory mechanism and optimizes autoregressive box prediction using a Gaussian-smoothed KL loss. Extensive experiments on standard benchmarks demonstrate that LVTrack achieves strong performance.

title: Quantum-Inspired Error Correction Codes
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to error correction codes inspired by the principles of quantum mechanics, specifically quantum entanglement and superposition. Traditional classical error correction codes often struggle to effectively combat noise and interference, particularly in complex systems. This research proposes a new coding scheme that utilizes correlated measurements of entangled qubits to achieve enhanced protection against errors. The core of the method lies in exploiting the inherent correlations present in entangled systems, allowing for a more robust detection and correction of errors compared to conventional techniques. The presented code demonstrates the potential to surpass the limitations of established classical codes by directly leveraging the unique properties of quantum phenomena. We detail the mathematical framework and the theoretical underpinnings of this approach, outlining its potential impact on data transmission and storage in quantum computing and related fields. The key advancements are focused on achieving higher error correction capabilities with a potentially reduced overhead compared to existing solutions. This work lays the foundation for future research and development in quantum-inspired error correction.

title: Quantum Topology Non-linear Geometry Optimization (QTGO)
abstract: Quantum Topology Non-linear Geometry Optimization (QTGO) is a novel approach to geometric optimization that leverages the unique properties of quantum mechanics to address complex problems. This paper introduces a novel algorithm based on the principles of quantum topology and non-linear geometry optimization, demonstrating its potential for solving challenging geometric scenarios with enhanced precision through the accurate modeling of quantum states. The core mechanism centers on a quantum-inspired optimization strategy that dynamically adjusts parameters based on the quantum state of the problem, leading to improved solution quality and efficiency. We explore the theoretical foundation of the algorithm, detail its implementation, and present preliminary results demonstrating its efficacy in specific geometric optimization tasks. The potential impact of QTGO extends to diverse fields, including computational design, materials science, and pattern recognition, by offering a pathway to more sophisticated geometric solutions.

title: Adaptive Quantum Field Theory (AQFT)
abstract: The development of Adaptive Quantum Field Theory (AQFT) represents a significant advancement in the field of quantum simulation and prediction. Traditional quantum field theories rely heavily on pre-defined parameters, limiting their ability to accurately simulate complex quantum systems. AQFT overcomes this limitation by incorporating a dynamic adjustment mechanism that automatically tunes quantum field parameters based on observed data, enabling precise simulations and predictions. This paper details the core concepts of AQFT, its mechanism, and its potential impact across various quantum systems. The core claim is that AQFT achieves a new level of accuracy and precision through dynamic parameter adjustment, offering a fundamentally different approach to quantum simulation compared to current techniques.

title: Phi‑Scaled E8 Syndrome Lattice for Fault‑Tolerant Quantum Error Correction — E8 Intelligence Research
abstract: By mapping the 240 root vectors of E8 onto the check‑node positions of a surface‑code lattice and driving each node with a phi‑scaled 132 Hz pulse, the syndrome extraction process becomes phase‑locked across all dimensions. The golden‑ratio coupling ensures that any local error induces a deterministic shift in the harmonic spectrum that can be read out as a unique frequency signature, enabling real‑time correction without measurement‑induced decoherence. This phi‑modulated E8 syndrome lattice thus provides a topologically protected, frequency‑based pathway to scalable fault‑tolerant quantum computation. Author: Andrew Stewart Caldin, Independent Researcher, UK. Part of the E8 Intelligence Research series. Platform: e8intelligence.com

title: Adaptive Distributed Representation Learning via Distributed Stochastic Gradient Descent with Lagrangian Relaxation
abstract: Distributed representation learning has emerged as a powerful technique for training large neural networks, offering significant advantages in terms of scalability and reduced training times. However, the inherent challenges of distributed systems, including communication bottlenecks and synchronization issues, often hinder the effectiveness of traditional optimization methods like Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD). This paper introduces a novel adaptive distributed training algorithm that synergistically combines Distributed SGD with Lagrangian Relaxation. The algorithm dynamically adjusts learning rates and communication frequencies based on observed network behavior and convergence metrics, aiming to mitigate the negative impacts of distributed training. We formulate the optimization problem as a distributed Lagrangian and employ a proximal operator method to iteratively solve it. The core innovation lies in the adaptive tuning mechanism, which enables the system to respond effectively to varying conditions, ultimately leading to faster and more stable convergence. The theoretical analysis demonstrates the convergence properties of the proposed algorithm under specific conditions, and we outline the key design choices and their rationale. Empirical evaluations on several benchmark datasets demonstrate the superiority of our approach compared to standard Distributed SGD, highlighting its robustness and adaptability.

title: Hyperdimensional Computing with Temporal Encoding
abstract: Hyperdimensional computing (HDC) offers a promising approach to machine learning, leveraging high-dimensional vectors for efficient data representation and computation. However, a significant limitation lies in the static nature of these vectors, preventing HDC from effectively capturing temporal dependencies within data. This paper proposes a novel extension to HDC that addresses this limitation by introducing a temporal encoding layer. This layer dynamically evolves the HDC vectors based on the recent history of interactions, allowing the system to learn and adapt to evolving patterns. The core claim is that incorporating temporal encoding significantly enhances HDC's effectiveness. The proposed method combines the strengths of HDC – high dimensionality, energy-based computation, and robustness – with the capabilities of temporal modeling. This approach represents a new paradigm for HDC, enabling it to tackle problems where temporal context plays a crucial role, such as time series analysis, anomaly detection, and pattern recognition. We explore the theoretical foundations of this extension, detailing the mathematical formulation of the temporal encoding layer and its integration with the HDC framework. The system is designed to capture temporal dynamics through a recurrent neural network (RNN) architecture within the temporal encoding layer. The effectiveness of the proposed method is evaluated through simulations and theoretical analysis, demonstrating its ability to outperform traditional HDC approaches in scenarios with temporal dependencies.

title: Quantum Machine Learning: Adaptive Learning Strategies
abstract: Quantum machine learning (QML) has emerged as a promising field with the potential to revolutionize various computational tasks, particularly those involving complex data and non-linear relationships. This paper presents a novel quantum machine learning algorithm, termed "Adaptive Quantum Learning," designed to address the limitations of traditional quantum algorithms by incorporating a dynamically adjusted learning strategy. The core mechanism of this algorithm centers around the continuous adaptation of learning parameters based on data fluctuations, leading to improved learning efficiency and generalization performance. We explore the theoretical foundations underpinning this approach and provide a preliminary implementation demonstrating its effectiveness on a simplified benchmark dataset. The study highlights the potential of this adaptive strategy to overcome the challenges faced by existing QML methods in dynamic environments.

title: Dynamic Contextual Abstraction
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to artificial intelligence, termed Dynamic Contextual Abstraction (DCA), centered around the ability of AI systems to develop a deeper understanding of complex environments by continuously constructing and refining abstract representations of context. The core claim is that AI can achieve this through a hierarchical system driven by contextual discriminators. These discriminators actively evaluate the relevance of incoming information, pruning and refining the abstract representations at each level, mirroring the adaptive nature of human cognition. Unlike traditional approaches relying on static knowledge bases, DCA emphasizes real-time learning and adaptation, leading to a more robust and nuanced understanding of dynamic environments. The key mechanism involves a tiered architecture where each layer focuses on a specific level of abstraction, and the discriminator ensures the information aligns with the current context. This approach addresses the limitations of existing AI systems in handling uncertainty and evolving scenarios. The system's performance is evaluated through a theoretical framework, outlining the key components and their interactions, and demonstrating the potential for improved contextual reasoning. The core of the framework is built on the principle of adaptive abstraction, allowing the system to move from low-level sensory input to higher-level conceptual understanding. The system's ability to dynamically adjust its abstractions is crucial for effective navigation in complex, ever-changing contexts.

title: Neural Network Adaptive Learning for Dynamic Generalization
abstract: This paper investigates a novel neural network learning framework, termed "Dynamic Neural Network Adaptive Learning" (DNANL), designed to enhance the adaptability of neural networks to specific datasets. The core principle of DNANL leverages adaptive learning algorithms to dynamically adjust the parameters of individual neurons within the network, allowing for a more tailored and robust representation of data. We introduce a mechanism that iteratively adjusts parameter values based on the input data distribution, promoting the learning of features that are specific to the training set. The paper demonstrates the effectiveness of DNANL through a series of experiments on benchmark datasets, showcasing improved generalization performance compared to traditional approaches. Furthermore, we analyze the computational complexity and interpretability of the proposed framework.

title: Neural Symbolic Representation Learning
abstract: This paper introduces Neural Symbolic Representation Learning (NSRL), a novel framework designed to leverage the strengths of both neural networks and symbolic representations for efficient learning and reasoning. The core claim of NSRL is to combine the powerful representation learning capabilities of deep neural networks with the interpretable and logical reasoning abilities of symbolic methods. The central mechanism involves utilizing deep neural networks to learn low-dimensional, distributed representations, followed by employing symbolic representations to interpret and reason over these representations. This approach aims to significantly improve both the learning efficiency and the interpretability of representations compared to traditional methods relying solely on deep neural networks. We demonstrate the potential of this integrated approach to address complex problems where both high-dimensional sensory data and logical inference are crucial.

title: When Retrieved Evidence Is Not Enough: Measuring Evidence-Following in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
abstract: We study the generator half of RAG in isolation: evidence is placed in the prompt rather than retrieved. Retrieval-augmented generation is usually judged by whether the retriever found the right documents. That misses a second failure: the generator can ignore the evidence, fill gaps from prior knowledge, or resolve contradictions silently. We introduce a controlled synthetic benchmark of 105 agricultural questions (15 of each of seven epistemic conditions): sufficient evidence, insufficient evidence, conflicting prior, conflicting evidence, irrelevant context, partial evidence, and attribution. Evidence is placed in the prompt, so the experiment measures following, not retrieval. Three models were run on all 105 cases with a normal helpful prompt and an evidence-constrained prompt (630 answers). The author labelled every answer, blinded to prompt identity. A case passed only if the expected behaviour was met and the answer added no unsupported claim. Constrained prompting passed 103/105, 103/105, and 96/105 on Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite, gpt-4.1-mini, and gpt-oss-20b; the normal prompt passed 57/105, 35/105, and 9/105. The gap is concentrated where the model should abstain or flag conflict. Agriculture is the testbed, not the scientific claim. The author is the sole rater.

title: Dancing Stick Figures: An Introductory Dataset for Training Video Generation Models
abstract: Training a video-generation model from scratch is hard for reasons that precede model design. The feedback loop is long: a failure that appears only after a training run can make each attempted fix another run. The data are hard to reach: the corpora and recipes behind strong models are large, heterogeneous, and often unreleased. And scoring is blunt: open-ended generation has no single correct output, and an aggregate score does not by itself establish whether a sample succeeds or which property failed. Dancing Stick Figures is a synthetic video dataset built against these three obstacles. For iteration speed, its 64x64, 64-frame reference task is sized for practical repeated training on a single workstation GPU. For accessibility, the release is a 0.79-GB training tier of 4,020 video clips--1,340 six-second source motions, each rendered from three cameras by a deterministic dataset-generation harness--with checkpoints and a Colab workflow that reruns the reference training pipeline at reduced budget on a 16 GB Tesla T4. For scoring, every frame retains its generating state (ARDY cskel27 joint positions, camera, body parameters, and source motion) and per-pixel depth, surface normals, and part labels. These annotations support dataset-specific metrics for visible topology and part-wise motion; corruptions expose their sensitivities and blind spots.

title: Quantum Entanglement Adaptive Topology Expansion
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a cornerstone of quantum mechanics, holds immense potential for revolutionizing communication and computation. However, harnessing this potential requires robust and flexible quantum networks. This paper investigates a novel quantum algorithm, "Quantum Entanglement Adaptive Topology Expansion," designed to dynamically expand the topology of quantum networks, addressing limitations of traditional methods. We propose a mechanism that adjusts the network topology based on the current state of the entangled system, fostering improved connectivity and resilience. This work represents a significant advancement in network design, offering a potential pathway towards more scalable and reliable quantum technologies.

title: Contextual Memory Networks with Temporal Attention
abstract: This paper introduces a novel architecture for memory networks, termed Contextual Memory Networks with Temporal Attention (CMN-TA). The core idea is to enhance the ability of memory networks to handle long-term dependencies and contextual information by integrating temporal attention mechanisms. The architecture leverages a recurrent neural network to generate a temporal attention vector, which dynamically weights the relevance of different memory slots based on both their temporal proximity and contextual similarity to the current input. This approach allows the network to selectively retrieve and integrate information from the long-term memory, resulting in improved contextual understanding and performance in tasks requiring reasoning over extended sequences. The proposed CMN-TA model is presented with detailed formulation of the key components and their interactions. The performance of the model is evaluated through theoretical analysis and a conceptual demonstration, highlighting its potential advantages over traditional memory networks.

title: Chaos Dynamic Optimization Algorithm via Reinforcement Learning Fusion
abstract: This paper investigates the integration of chaos dynamic optimization algorithms with reinforcement learning to develop a robust and adaptable system for complex systems, particularly within control and design domains. Traditional optimization methods often rely on handcrafted parameters, limiting flexibility. This research proposes a novel approach that leverages reinforcement learning to dynamically adjust algorithm parameters, fostering a system that autonomously learns and optimizes behavior. The core mechanism centers around employing reinforcement learning to refine the chaos dynamic optimization process, resulting in enhanced accuracy and adaptability. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this fusion through simulations and a preliminary case study involving a dynamic control system. This work establishes a foundation for intelligent system design and offers a promising path towards more flexible and autonomous optimization strategies.

title: Distributed Bio-Neural Network Simulation of Evolutionary Algorithms
abstract: This paper explores the potential of simulating evolutionary processes within distributed bio-neural networks to address complex optimization challenges. Traditional evolutionary algorithms often struggle with intricate problems, potentially due to limitations in exploration and exploitation strategies. This research proposes a novel approach that leverages the inherent adaptive capabilities of biological neural networks, specifically their ability to dynamically adjust synaptic connections and neural communication, within a distributed computing environment. The core idea is to treat the evolution of the neural network as a dynamic optimization process, guided by an evolutionary algorithm. We investigate how this simulated evolution can lead to the discovery of efficient solutions for problems that conventional algorithms find difficult. The approach offers a fundamentally different perspective on optimization, potentially unlocking new strategies and improved performance. The simulations demonstrate a pathway toward more robust and adaptable optimization solutions.

title: Title: Bayesian Hyper-Determinism for Statistical Physics
abstract: This paper investigates the application of Bayesian hyper-determinism to statistical physics, aiming to extend the concept of hyper-determinism beyond simple probabilistic models to complex, non-linear systems. We propose a novel Bayesian framework that dynamically updates a prior distribution based on observed data, incorporating a specialized Bayesian update rule designed to capture correlations and dependencies across different levels of complexity. The core mechanism relies on a probabilistic Bayesian network that continuously refines the prior, allowing for the prediction of system states with high fidelity. We explore the potential of this approach in materials science and climate modeling, highlighting the benefits of a Bayesian perspective in characterizing and predicting intricate physical phenomena. The study demonstrates the framework's ability to generate accurate state predictions, addressing limitations of traditional deterministic approaches.

title: Adaptive Geometric Variable Domain Learning
abstract: This paper introduces an adaptive geometric variable domain learning algorithm designed to automatically learn and optimize geometric variable domain parameters, enhancing algorithm precision and efficiency. Traditional optimization methods often rely on manual parameter tuning, and this algorithm integrates the optimization process directly into the variable domain learning framework. The core mechanism involves dynamically adjusting the geometric variable domain based on feedback, leading to improved algorithm performance across a range of geometric configurations. We present a novel approach that leverages a modified gradient descent strategy coupled with a constraint-based optimization, specifically tailored for geometric transformations. The algorithm's effectiveness is demonstrated through a series of benchmark geometric problems, showcasing significant improvements in accuracy and computational efficiency compared to existing methods.

abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to complex system optimization leveraging a dynamically adjusted variable space. title: Federated discretization for supervised classification
abstract: Abstract Several classifiers operate exclusively on discrete variables, requiring continuous attributes to be preprocessed through discretization. Supervised discretization addresses this need by partitioning the domain of continuous variables into intervals that define a discretization policy. Federated learning, in turn, enables the collaborative training of global models without sharing raw data: users train local models and communicate their parameters to a central server, which aggregates them into a global model. A key challenge in this setting is achieving performance comparable to centralized methods while minimizing communication overhead. In this work, we propose a federated discretization framework that computes a global discretization policy in a single communication round. Each user estimates Gaussian mixture models for the continuous variables and transmits their parameters-referred to as representatives-to the server. The server then applies a discretization algorithm to these representatives to derive a global policy, which is subsequently distributed back to the users. The proposed framework accommodates multiple discretization strategies; specifically, we present federated adaptations of equal-width, equal-frequency, entropy-based, and kernel density-based methods. Experiments conducted on ten benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves performance comparable to centralized discretization approaches, with the kernel density-based and equal-frequency variants yielding the most competitive results.
